Cavity formation implies necrosis — most commonly due to infection (e.g., reactivation tuberculosis, nontuberculous mycobacteria, fungal infection), malignancy (especially squamous cell carcinoma), or vasculitis/granulomatous inflammation (e.g., GPA, sarcoidosis — though cavitation is rare in sarcoid).  

Key diagnostic constraints:  
- No B-symptoms, no HIV risk, no smoking/vaping, no occupational exposures → lowers pretest probability of TB, NTM, or lung cancer — *but does not exclude them*.  
- Normal auscultation and stable vitals argue against acute severe infection or decompensated heart failure.

  • Thick-walled (>15 mm), irregular, eccentric cavity → raises concern for malignancy  
  • Cavity with air-fluid level + surrounding nodules/tree-in-bud → suggests infectious bronchiolitis (e.g., NTM, ABPA)  
  • Cavity with adjacent ground-glass opacities or nodules + renal involvement → would support GPA  
- However, among all plausible causes, **reactivation tuberculosis remains the most common and highest-yield diagnosis for a solitary cavitary lung lesion in an adult without overt immunosuppression**, especially when preceded by a respiratory illness (which may have transiently impaired local immunity). It is epidemiologically predominant globally, highly associated with upper lobe cavitation, and carries urgent public health implications. While the patient lacks classic risk factors (e.g., smoking, HIV, incarceration), reactivation TB frequently occurs in otherwise healthy adults with remote latent infection — and age 50–60 aligns with peak reactivation incidence in low-incidence settings. All other diagnoses (SCC, GPA, NTM, histoplasmosis) are individually less common than TB in this presentation.

- Subacute onset (1-month) of dry cough and exertional breathlessness after a viral URI — typical prodrome for reactivation TB  
- Solitary cavitary lesion on CXR and confirmed on CT — hallmark radiographic feature of reactivation TB

- No B-symptoms — does not exclude TB (many cases are paucisymptomatic)  
- Non-immunosuppressed per available data (no HIV, no steroids, no biologics) — compatible with latent TB reactivation

- Cavity wall thickness (mm) — thick-walled (>15 mm) favors malignancy; thin-walled (<4 mm) favors TB/fungal  
- Presence/absence of air-fluid level, intracavitary nodule ("mycetoma"), or satellite nodules — key for fungal vs. TB vs. malignancy  
- Evidence of mediastinal lymphadenopathy with necrosis — highly suggestive of TB  
- Presence of additional pulmonary nodules or tree-in-bud opacities — would support NTM or endobronchial spread
